newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. warns against arms in Zaire refugee camp.
newsitem.headline: U.N. warns against arms in Zaire refugee camp.

text.p: The new U.N. special envoy for Central Africa, Mohammed Sahnoun, arrived in Zaire on Saturday with the world body warning that the arming of Rwandan Hutu hardliners could turn a refugee camp there into a battleground.

U.N. officials in New York said that Sahnoun, who arrived from the Rwandan capital Kigali, would pass a message of concern to the Kinshasa government from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan about the plight of refugees in Zaire's civil war zone.

Both Annan and the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata have warned that Rwandan Hutu civilians clustered around the village of Tingi Tingi could be the main victims if Hutu hardliners make a stand there against Tutsi-led rebels.
But a senior Kinshasa defence ministry official told Reuters that Zaire was not arming the Hutu hardliners, who have been blamed for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis.
"They say we have given weapons to the Hutu hardliners there but how can we do this when we have weaponry problems with our own troops," he said, dismissing the charge as rebel propaganda.
Up to 150,000 refugees occupy makeshift camps around Tingi Tingi, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Zaire's third city of Kisangani, headquarters for army operations against the rebels.
Medical workers say up to 30 people a day are dying in Tingi Tingi from hunger or disease. The Zairean official said there were no reports of fighting from the area on Saturday.
Annan appealed to all parties "to stop turning the Tingi Tingi refugee camp into an armed base and to ensure the safety and security of all refugees and humanitarian personnel".
He said ex-Rwandan Hutu soldiers and militias there were receiving arms and ammunition by air and were being sent to frontlines or deploying near the camps.
"This situation puts at risk the lives of innocent refugees and humanitarian workers in the area," he said, adding that young male refugees were being actively recruited.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said following an appeal from Ogata he had ordered his forces to avoid the Tingi Tingi.
But Ogata, speaking in Tanzania, remained very concerned. "When it becomes an area of militarised activities, the camp could easily become a target of military attack," she said.

Ethnic Tutsis launched the war in October, accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and of plans to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home. They now hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.

Rebel thrusts on several fronts have blunted a counter-offensive the army launched on January 20 but the army says no major towns have fallen and it is reinforcing Kisangani and Buta to the north and Kindu to the south.
Kabila has given President Mobutu Sese Seko, who spent half of last year in France recovering from prostate surgery, until February 21 to begin talks on stepping down.

Supporters of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, meanwhile, postponed a rally at their Kinshasa headquarters on Saturday, one day after the government banned public demonstrations. They said security conditions were not right.
A strike called by Tshisekedi supporters on Monday to demand the removal of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo virtually shut down the usually teeming capital of five million people.
